title: Bamidbar: set apart to serve (Numbers 3:12)
hookLine: the tribe of Levi is set apart to serve the sanctuary

cards: In some synagogues, just before the priestly blessing, a few people slip out and come back with a pitcher and a basin.

They pour water over the hands of the kohanim, the priests' descendants, who are about to bless the congregation. Then the kohanim go up front, and the pourers go back to their seats. No speech, no spotlight.
Ask who they are, and you'll often hear: they're Levites. Some families named Levi, Levine, Levy or Halevi carry that tribe in their name.

teach.b: Numbers chapter three. God tells Moses that the Levites will be taken instead of every firstborn of Israel, "and the Levites shall be Mine."
Back in Egypt, the firstborn had been spared on the night of the plague, and so they belonged to God. Now a whole tribe takes their place.
Rashi links the choice to the golden calf: when Moses called out who is on the LORD's side, the tribe of Levi came. Levi's name comes from the story of his birth in Genesis.
His mother Leah hoped that now her husband would be joined to her.
Levi, joined. And that's the job. Aaron's family within the tribe are the priests, who offer at the altar.

The rest of the Levites are joined to them: they guard the Tabernacle, take it down, carry its pieces through the desert, and set it up again. Later, in the Temple, the Bible remembers them as singers and gatekeepers.
They get no portion of land like the other tribes; they live in cities scattered among everyone else. Their inheritance, the Torah says elsewhere, is God.
In synagogues today, a Levite is customarily called second to the Torah reading, and at the priestly blessing, Levites may wash the priests' hands. And Maimonides widens the door.
Not only the tribe of Levi, he writes, but any person whose spirit moves them to stand before God and serve becomes holy.
The role is inherited. The calling is open.

how: In many synagogues a Levite is called second to the Torah reading, after a kohen, and Levites wash the hands of the kohanim before the priestly blessing. Some families with names like Levi, Levine or Halevi trace descent from the tribe.

o: joined: the tribe that serves the sanctuary
the firstborn sons spared in Egypt
Aaron's family, who offer at the altar

games.q: the tribe set apart — tap the pairs.

s: only Aaron's family were priests; the other Levites guarded, carried and served.
the Levites received no tribal portion of land
they lived in cities scattered among the other tribes.
Maimonides says only Levites can be set apart to serve God
he writes that anyone whose spirit moves them to serve becomes holy.

games.q: the firstborn of Israel were spared in Egypt and belong to God. in the wilderness, who takes their place in serving the sanctuary?
o: the tribe of Judah, which leads the march.
games.why: "and the Levites shall be Mine." Rashi links it to the golden calf, when the Levites came to Moses' side.

practice: Look around your life for the pourers of water: the person who sets out chairs before the meeting and stacks them after, the one who refills the coffee and remembers the birthdays, the custodian, the volunteer who never gives the speech.
Pick one face and hold it for a while. Notice how much of your week rests on work like theirs.

wordCard.voice: Levi. Joined: the tribe set apart to guard, carry and serve the sanctuary, with no land of its own.

orig.note: Hebrew: Levi. Leah named him hoping her husband would be joined to her.

carryVoice: Your line: set apart to serve. Quiet work holds the whole camp together. That's day four hundred thirty-three.

sources.q: and the Levites shall be Mine
